title: Women Hold Just 11% of Management Jobs in Japan
paragraphs: Japan has been trying to get more women into leadership roles at work. But a new survey shows that progress is still very slow.
The survey was carried out by Teikoku Databank, a Japanese research company, in July. More than 10,000 companies answered questions about women in their workplaces.

The survey found that, on average, women make up only 11.3% of managers at Japanese companies. This is the highest number ever recorded in the survey, but it is just 0.2 points higher than last year. In other words, the number is growing very slowly.
At many Japanese companies, there are no women managers at all. In fact, companies where all the managers are men were the largest group, making up 42.1% of companies in the survey.

The numbers were a little higher for the very top leaders. Women made up 14.2% of executives, which is 0.4 points higher than last year. However, more than half of Japanese companies still have no women executives.
The Japanese government has set a goal of having women in around 30% of management positions as soon as possible. The new results show that Japan is still far from reaching this goal.

Japan is also behind many other countries. According to a separate survey by the accounting company Grant Thornton, women hold 21.5% of senior management positions at mid-sized companies in Japan. The global average is 32.9%.

Different surveys measure this in different ways, so the exact numbers can vary. However, they all show the same thing: women are still a small minority among leaders at Japanese companies, and change is happening only slowly.
